Supported: Robbins has said in interviews (HuffPost, Worth) that watching people suffer in 2008 made him decide to write the book and recalled his childhood when people could not afford food; the book is built on interviews with leading financial figures including Ray Dalio, John Bogle, Carl Icahn and Paul Tudor Jones (named in several sources); its stated aim is to give ordinary investors access to strategies large institutions use. The count of fifty interviewees rests on one site, so it is omitted. The Bogle 45-minutes-turned-four-and-a-half-hours story is repeated in secondary sources and may come from interviews, not the book: omitted. Interview statements are attributed to Robbins, not claimed as book text. No direct quotes. The 'question' framing is the writer's reading of the book's stated aim, not a supported fact. The one-line descriptions of who the interviewees are come from general knowledge, not from the book. Interview-sourced, not book text: Inside Job, 'the system has to change'.
facts: Money: Master the Game came out in 2014.
Robbins has said that the 2008 financial crisis, and the suffering he saw among people, is why he wrote it.
He has said the crisis reminded him of his childhood, when people could not afford food.
He had long been known as a coach on performance, not as a finance writer.
For the book he sat down with leading financial figures, among them Ray Dalio, John Bogle, Carl Icahn and Paul Tudor Jones.
Dalio explains his all-weather style of portfolio; Bogle represents the case for index funds.
The stated aim of the book is to hand ordinary investors strategies that big institutions use.
The book's subtitle promises seven simple steps to financial freedom.
Robbins had coached Paul Tudor Jones for years, which helped him reach some interviewees (secondary source, hedged).

Background about the interviewees (general knowledge, not the book's account): Dalio founded the investment firm Bridgewater; Bogle founded the fund company Vanguard and championed index funds; Icahn is known as an activist investor; Tudor Jones founded a hedge-fund firm.
Robbins has said the documentary Inside Job deepened his frustration with how the crisis was handled (Worth, secondary).
Robbins has said he concluded that the system had to change (HuffPost interview).
scene_details: interviews with Ray Dalio, John Bogle, Carl Icahn and Paul Tudor Jones
ordinary savers on one side, institutions on the other
tension: A motivational coach answers a financial crisis by going to interview the people who run money.
opening_idea: Open on the list of people Robbins sat down with (Dalio, Bogle, Icahn, Tudor Jones), a strange guest list for a motivational coach.

lessons.idea: When something goes badly wrong in a field you do not know, go and ask the people who know it best, and ask on behalf of those with less access.
lessons.anchor: Robbins taking his questions to Dalio, Bogle, Icahn and Tudor Jones

reflect_final: Which area of your life are you still handling by guesswork that you could improve by asking one person who does it very well?

use_cases.situation: You do not understand your pension statement.
use_cases.move: Ask someone who handles money well to walk through it with you, and bring two questions.

use_cases.situation: A friend is anxious about their savings.
use_cases.move: Say Robbins went and asked specialists after 2008, and offer to find one name you could both ask.

use_cases.situation: Your team has a gap nobody in it can fill.
use_cases.move: Name one outside person who does this well and ask for twenty minutes.

pocket_idea: After 2008 Robbins went to ask Dalio, Bogle and others: when you lack the answer, borrow it from those who hold it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: After the 2008 crisis, a motivational coach went to interview Ray Dalio and John Bogle about money.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Tony Robbins is known for peak performance, not finance. After 2008, he says, seeing people suffer pushed him to write Money: Master the Game. He sat down with figures like Ray Dalio, John Bogle and Carl Icahn, and wrote the book to give ordinary investors what big institutions already use.
